chapter: Later tours, illness and the union job
title: European audiences versus American ones
summary: Clayton and Dance discuss why European fans are more appreciative, including Ellington's rare visits.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Well, you've probably had more experience in Europe than most American musicians who've been over there because I mean you lived there a long time. Did you find a short of big difference in the audiences as compared with those here?

Oh yes. All the difference in the world. You know there is, there is fans here that are just as great to you I think. Now you take the Duke Ellington fan club, you know that club, they're all dedicated fans, especially of Duke's. But it seems to me that all the people over there are that way, not just a few. There is some fans here like Jim Dunn in Connecticut, all of the Duke fans but over there everybody is that way, you know? And they just appreciate you so much. They give you so much more applause, that you have to be kind of careful. I've seen guys go over there and get the big head, they think they're so much greater. I've seen drummers and trombone players
you can't speak to them after they've been to Europe. They come back here and they want to be treated like they are over there and they don't.

Yes, well I've always thought that one reason for that is that jazz is taken for granted here more, which is natural. Because I mean, you think as far as England is concerned, Duke Ellington came there in 1933 and he did not come back with the band because of union problems and the War, he did not come back until 25 years later.

Now, this is the sort of thing that people over there remember you know. So Coleman Hawkins goes or somebody like that and Jimmie Lunceford went to Europe just once. Well people just sort of had the feeling well you'd better see him because who knows when he might be back? Whereas here, if Duke were playing in Newark we'll say, or Philadelphia and you'd already arranged to play bridge that night, you'd obviously think, well he'll be back six months from now.
That does make a difference in attitude I think.
Yes, I guess so. I guess so. Because you can catch him at the Rainbow Grill or somewhere else.
If you don't do it now you can do it maybe in the next two or three months.
You think you can, you may be wrong in that, but I think it's natural here the tendency is to think that way.
